title: Laurena Diggs and Carrie Boote Interview, 1960-09-03

blocks.x: And we're going to start another interview. So Ms. Diggs, let me get your name again while the tape machine is on. Lorena Diggs. L-A-U-R-E-N-A. And your name again? Carrie Boop. And I'm Dick Allen again. And we just finished doing an interview with Archie Martin. And we're still up here at 1926 Harmony Street, September the 3rd, 1960. Alright, so... I have a whole lot of questions to ask you all about. Ms. Diggs, do you mind telling me about that song, Over the Garden Wall? Do you remember we were talking about that the other day?

Yeah. Well, I'll tell you, it's been quite a while. Because I heard the last of it was in, when was I in Milwaukee, in 40-something. That was the last, but that was when during the Spanish-American War. Over the Golden Wall, the sweetest girl of all. I'll never forget the night we met over the Golden Wall. That's what that was. Goodbye, dear one, till we meet again over the Golden Wall. I'll never forget the night we met over the Golden Wall. Now that was sang in the Spanish-American War. Mm-hmm.
You know, when I talked to you before, I listened to the tape again, you know. It seemed like I left some things out. Do you remember when they started doing that second line dancing in Mobile?
The, um, well, let me see. I, no, I can't remember what we were dancing there, the, um.
No, I mean following the parades.
Wait, I'll see that. I can't remember. Oh, the, oh, mm, that was the Lions Band, but I can't remember now what it was.
The Lions Band used to come over there and play parades?
Yeah, from here. The Lions Band.
Now, uh, they had the Excelsior over there, you said?
The Excelsior was a real band, but the Lions was when we'd have the parade, had more jazz music to it.
Mm-hmm. Well, what did the people do when the jazz music started playing in the street?
Mm-hmm. Just like they did here, they would prance and dance and go on.
They would carry on just like they did in New Orleans? Mm-hmm. They'd carry on just like they did in New Orleans? Yes. Now, that Lions Band, uh, when did it start coming to Mobile?
Well, uh, well, uh, I was about, uh, 21 or 22 long in that, and I'm 89 now. Mm-hmm.

Well, that was making in, uh, about 94, say around 95, that their Lions started coming over there. Yes. Before that, when the Excelsior played in the Eureka Band of Mobile, those local musicians over there, were the people prancing the street at all?
Well, they did, but not as much as they did when the bands come from here that had more jazz to it. They did. They did.
I see. So that was definitely a difference, yeah.
Mm-hmm.
There was a difference in the music in Mobile and New Orleans. Yes. Now, uh, what year did you first come to New Orleans, even on a visit?
Mm-hmm. How do you remember? When I first come to New Orleans, I was five years old. When I first come to New Orleans, I was five years old. When I first come to New Orleans, I was five years old.
And what do you remember about New Orleans?

What I remember about that time, was a small, little wood, deep wood canal and the river. And my mother and father and I walked right down the railroad to the, what do you call it, the railroad yard, railroad shop. I was five years old. And they had one mule car. They used to have one mule to a car. And we walked right straight from that canal and the river, right straight up to the railroad shop. My father was transferred here from Mobile. And I went home and come back and went to school here in Long and about 19 and something. I'll tell you, the day that we get to do, the time to put up the Leeds Circle at Redport, at St. Charles, well, we were there. Saying, we praise him, we praise him, all of the nation, for his mercy and his kindness. He's great to all of us. Well, I was in school then, the white and colored, we went there. There was nothing but woods, trees, big old rocks in the street, and horse cars. I understand.
Did white and colored go to the same school?

Yeah, no, no, but we had all, most of the white teachers. Most of the white teachers that all owned private schools. Maroney, Claiborne, and the fifth school, all of those were white teachers when I went to those three. Maroney's, Claiborne and Maroney, just a few blocks on the other side of Lydgenfield. And Claiborne, St. Peter and Claiborne. And the fifth school is the last school that I went to, Perdita and Franklin. That was the last school I went to here. We would march from there, out Perdita Street to St. Charles, white and colored, singing. We praise him, we praise him, all of the nation, for his mercy and his kindness. He was great. And they just have ropes, and just going around singing and pulling him up. That lead circle down there. Yeah, that's what's, oh, let's see it. All I need to do is to see the red top, and I think it's, I'll put it down. Yeah, that's my last schooling.
So you came here in 78 the first time, and you didn't stay long?
No, my husband didn't stay here very long. Then we went back home and come again. But our first time was, I was just five years old.
Your second time when you came how old?
Well, I was about, oh, well, about 12 or 13 years old. During at that time.
So that would be about 1885 or so. 18. 85, 86, along there.
See, well anyhow, for as long of that time I was in my teens when they come back. We went to Maroney School.
And did you stay much here then?
Yes, stayed here until way under. I was about 16 and we went back home to live all together.
And you stayed over in Mobile for how long? When you were 16 you stayed for a long time?
Until 19 and 16.
You got here right after the big storm then?
Yeah, in the storm we come here. In this storm right at Washington and Ramport. We come here from Moluccio in that storm.

But Mama didn't, you didn't stay over there all the time because I was born then and Mama used to be here every month or so. I mean, we weren't living here but we used to be here all the time. Because I was born then and I know I had been here I don't know how many times during that time. When you mean we come to live? I know when we came back to live. I know when we came back to live but I mean you made I guess hundreds of visits. Oh yes, right. Yeah. Because you visit over here quite often.
When did they start playing jazz and Mobile?

Well I'll tell you sir, I haven't been around into the jazz and Mobile in quite a number of years to take part. But only known of these bands going from here over there at that time. The excursions used to go from here and the alliances and the other bands would play there. But I didn't take great part in it in the younger days, no, because then I had married and of course it would be a great pleasure for me to go here, there, on the excursions. And they would have a picnic and play. The people would highly enjoy these people here because they had more jazz music it seemed like in the boys.

Well they called it string bands and those other bands were brass bands. Now the brass bands, they didn't play that hot type of music. You know, that music was a difference in the string band and the brass band. So at that time I don't think they were calling it jazz bands, they were calling it string bands. But it was all on the order of jazz music. That's the way I see it because they call it a string band and a brass band. But the string band played hotter music, you know. It's more exciting I guess than those brass bands. Because they had a large group in the brass band. I don't know how many men, but in the string band they didn't have so many, you know, white clings.
So when you were growing up, you were in Mobile Park.

I don't know anything about Mobile. I was born there, but we were raised here. We were raised here. We came here the week after the September storm. Was it some storm? I don't know. Not the September storm. Another big storm. The Hedgesher. Yeah, it was September, huh? But I know I was quite a small girl. I did. And all my growing up were here. I don't know anything about Mobile because we were small when we left there. But I know more about here than I know more real, see. I see.
Well, I'm going to sit out there. You want to get outside, mister? No, no. I was just telling her that she know what I was speaking about. Oh, I see. I'm looking for a letter for my son.
Oh, yeah. Yeah. What time did the veterans of the Spanish-American War go down to Chalmette? You were telling me about that.

The time did they go down? What time of the year? In May, the last of May. But we don't go down there anymore now. But we used to have a grand celebration. In the last of May. That was the 30th, isn't it? A holiday on the 31st of May? 31st of May. 30th, something.
Yeah. So, you go one day, excuse me, one day a year only?
Yes, that's our celebration of one day. Of course, we go hardly any time, but that would be the great day we go. 31st in the last of May.
Now, I was going to ask you about the art fellows and the benevolent associations and the societies and clubs and things. Did they have them in Mobile?
Oh, yes. Have them just the same and have the Spanish-American War grand armor there just like we had here.
Did they use the brass bands over there in the parade?

Yes. The brass bands in our parade. Let me see. Yeah, we had the same way, of course. We had the Spanish-American War and the grand armor celebrated to have a ceremony, the last of May, like that we did here. You understand? Well, I belonged to it and my mother did too. My mother belonged to it there all of her life and I belonged to it after I became a big grown woman.
Well, over there, what would the brass bands play when the societies were out? What would the brass bands play over there? What would they play? Yeah, what kind of music?

Oh, well, I can't remember now what kind of music, but it would be a sad march. I can't think of it now. That we'd play for the opening and the closing, just like we had here. And I can't remember that.

Well, that's enough. That's all I want to know. They play sad music. They play sad, slow music. Yes. Now, did they bury with bands of music in Mobile? Yes. What would they do when they come back in Mobile?
They did jazz just like they did here. Just like they did here when they come back from there.
When did they start that custom? Huh? When did they start that custom?
I come found it when I grew up. I found that all along the bands carrying the dead out and bringing them back, but they didn't have that jazz fast music when they come back. Mm-hmm.
But they... Mm-hmm. Mm-hmm. But they...
Like just to have here, people kept up with the bands going to the funeral and coming back. They had the jazz music.
I don't want to wear you out.
You ain't been wearing me out because I'm just taking the time and telling you. They'll say we're so glad to put it all over. Do you rock about it? That would be the band coming back.
Oh, yeah. Do you rock about it? What does that mean?

That was a dance. That was a dance. It's like these bands play the jazz when they've been coming on back to play the rock about it. Well, everybody knows as far as the bands like hell, you know, they would keep up with that music. They say, well, they're playing the jazz then. Yeah, they're glad you're going to do my rock about it. I can remember that, Lord. It's a shame just to unbear that man and come in with all that music. Yeah. Yeah.
Let's bother Miss Boots for a while now. Huh? Let's bother Miss Boots for a while now.

Miss Boots, she's a little girl. She'd be on stage singing. Alexander, I'll hear you say you're going away. I'm coming back someday. Sorry to tell you, Alexander. That's what Miss Boots was playing with.
That was a minstrel show we used to have. They called them minstrel shows then, you know. So I used to try to be an actress there. Mm-hmm.
What would you sing, Tiara?
Oh, well, I hated quite a few things I sang. Huh? Actually, it was quite a few things we used to sing, but I never heard them song before and

since. That's the truth. But they must have meant. I heard you say, Alexander, I heard you say you're going away, coming back. Sorry to hear you, Alexander. You should come running back someday. That's what Tiara used to sing on the stage. That's what Tiara used to sing. Yeah. And would be dancing like that. And the arts. You would pull it. Yeah. And all the day.
Well, all right. Let him.
Well, we'll get her to sing Dying Rag for us.
And those songs I never heard, but, you know, I don't know who composed them or what, but we were singing them then.

Well, Dollar Bill is pretty famous, you know. They still making records of that, but if you got a hunt for them, you know. Yeah. But that's still popular. How did Dying Rag go now? I wanted to get that as much as you could remember.
It says, honey, I'm sinking fast. Soon I will breathe my legs. Pever is very high. Doctor say I will die. I'm no longer something. Then I know it's a...
Listen.

I forgot how it went. No, I didn't know. Oh, my honey dear. I must be going to fear. I feel the... See? Stealing something in here. I can't get it together now, but it was... At the end, they said that's the Dying Rag.
I can't think of it. What about Dollar Bill? Do you remember any of that?
What was that? Now they say...
The man's name, Dollar Bill.

No. This song was about whenever you get lucky, and all things come your way. Hold on to every dollar, no matter what the people say. I know just what I'm saying. I've been all around the world, and the only friend that I have had was a good old Dollar Bill. If a friend say, Bill, let's have some wine, tell him no. If a friend say, Bill, let's have a good time, tell him no. Oh. And that's always I can go on that. Now that's a song I never heard, but we sang that in his minstrel shows. They might have been just made up, you know.
Mm-hmm.
And, um... Toot your horn, toot your horn. Yeah. Toot my... Toot your horn something, because I'm in a fog or something like that. Those are all those songs that, you know, that...
Yeah, I can't think of them all now,
because there's so many songs.
And Buddy Christian had some, too.
Yeah, he composed a... I forgot the name of... But he composed a song at my house, and I've forgotten it. He played since I was talking to you.
He used to... I heard that.
Yeah. Uh-huh. He passed since I was talking to you.
I went to New York the next month.
Yeah.
And looked for him, and he'd already passed when we were talking, but nobody knew it then.
Yeah, well, no, we didn't know it.
And, uh... Because Richard M. Jones has been dead quite a while.
Oh, yeah, yeah.
He wrote, I ain't gonna tell nobody.
I ain't gonna tell nobody about the dream I had last night. It was so fine. I was in paradise. Yeah, he... He wrote that song. Did you ever know, um... Freddy Kepler? You ever heard of him?
Plenty.
Yeah. He was a fine trumpet player. He used to be in Chicago. I think he passed in Chicago for a day to go.
Let's see. You know, Richard M. Jones never did copyright that
and nobody ain't gonna tell nobody? No.
Isn't that a funny thing? Because it's a pretty tune.
And he played it. You know, he used to play it all. I thought that it was...
Down here or up there?
Up there?
And all of them made a record
of it so good. And then he never did...
Well, they couldn't find a copyright.
Maybe not.
Do you remember Glover Compton?

Sure, I remember Glover Compton. But he spent quite a few years in Europe. You know, he was a piano player. But now he... At least I don't know if he's living. And he was in New Orleans. He'd open the lounge there on 51st Street. Mm-hmm.
Do you remember the Clock of Time? A tune called The Clock of Time?
What was that?
A tune called The Clock of Time.
Clock of Time.
It was written by Tony Jackson and Glover Compton.
No, I didn't know that.
And I think Glover's wife wrote it to him. Nettie.
Yeah.
You're such a pretty thing. Do you remember that? You're such a pretty thing. Might have been a bad lover.
He might have been all right,
but he wasn't such a pretty thing. But here over here,
this piano player, Walter Johnson, he died over in India somewhere. He married an Indian prince. He was... He used to play with Tate in Chicago. I know.
Teddy Weatherford.
Not Teddy Weatherford. His name was Johnson, wasn't he?
Well, I know Teddy Weatherford died over there in India, too. But that's a... Maybe somebody else. Walter Johnson.
Walter Johnson.
Might be the same guy with two names, too. You know, that happens, too.

No, well, he was a great musician and he went over there and he never did come back. He used to play with Tate. During the time, Lewis was playing with Tate. Well, that's the same guy. Yeah. Uh-huh. He married an Indian princess? I read that into Ebony since I was here. He had passed about... It must have been between 56 because since I've been here, I read about him passed. Did you know him well? Not too well. You know how you come in contact with people, but I didn't know him, you know, just personally to go about with him, but I knew of him because I'd been in company with him, you know, quite often.
Well, who was this guy? Jill Pruset or Gil or something? Pruset? I couldn't understand it on the tape. Uh... I think he was... Joe Pruset? Oh, that must be Joe Pruset.

Well, they lived in Mississippi. They had a brace band there, the Pickwick brace band, and it was two brothers, Joe Pruset and Eddie Pruset. They had a brace band in Morris Point, Mississippi. They used to come over here and play. You know, the bands used to travel around during that time. And they would parade around the street then in wagons, you know. What was it? Trucks or wagons? I don't remember. And they would, like they're going to have a dance at the Bulls, well, they would play on each corner, you know, as they advertised where they're going to play tonight.
That's what the Crusets did.
Well, they played for different... Anybody that wanted to have a dance, they were for high, but their band was a brace band. Yes, yes, yes.
Well, what about in Mississippi? What did the brass bands do over there? That's what you're speaking about.

Well, they had dance halls there and they played all up and down the coast, you know, just like if any kind of affair and they wanted music, well, they'd hire them. And just like if they wanted a string band, they'd send way over here for a string band on different occasions like Fourth of July or something like that. And different bands would exchange. They'd come over here and play and they'd go over there. But most people had began to get used to the string music and now those brass bands, their music wasn't, you know, was a different type of music than the string music.
But the brass bands in Moss Point played dances.
Yeah.
They would definitely play at dances. Yeah. And what else? Would there parades over there?
Well, they didn't do much parading over there. They didn't do no. They didn't bear with parades or anything in Moss Point. They just played Moss Led dances. I see.
Who were the Whitman sisters?

Well, they was one of the old show groups. You know, they had the minstrel shows and they had, they had traveled quite a lot over the United States with Whitman sisters. They had, I guess there was minstrels during that time, you know, when they traveled around. And of late, they all, when they went north, they were quite popular and now, it's about three left and one, she's a spiritualist and Alice and, I've forgotten all their names now, but they were quite well known all over the South here. How many were there? I think it was about four. Four.
And one was a spiritualist.
Yeah, she's a spiritualist in Chicago now. Essie, Alice, and they would come back. But they, they traveled with their own, own band and everything.
Well, what does a spiritualist do?

Well, the spiritualist, they, they have a church, but they're like those mediums. They read, you know, they claim they can read and see the future and all like this. And they preach too. because a lot of theatrical people and smart people, some of them take, gets it as a racket and some may be sincere, I couldn't say, but it, it's nice money in it.
See, did you ever know a fellow named Johnny Dodds? He talked about it a minute ago.
I didn't, I didn't know him personally, but I know of him.
Yeah. Yeah. His brother was a drummer.
Yeah.

Baby. Uh-huh. Did you know Bill Johnson? He played banjo and bass? Real bright fella? No, no, I didn't know Bill Johnson. Yeah, I just wonder because, you know, they all work together, try to straighten them out the way you might have heard them in Chicago. Johnny St. Cyr, did you know him?
I knew of him. I didn't know him.
He was with Doc Cook for a long time. Your mother Doc Cook.
Yeah, I knew Doc Cook. He was from here, I think, with him.
I don't think. Well, anyhow, he used to. He had a lot of New Orleans fellas.
Yeah, I thought he was from here.
You know a fella called Nora Dutry? The trombone player, Honoré Dutry, Nora. He was up there, you know. It was all King Oliver fellas,
you know,
like, and Zoo was with.
I know Zoo, he's a drummer.
Judy, yeah.

Uh-huh. Now, they had three legged sisters. One was married to Honest Whitman, you know, just to be, what did he play with Ethel Waters, Bill. They were from here, the legged sisters. They were popular show people that were married. One was married to Ernest Whitman.
Ernest Whitman played what?

Bill, with Ethel Waters, that series that they had on the radio. Oh, yeah, he was an actor. Yeah. And Hattie McDaniel, he used to play with her. Well, he was married to one of the legged sisters from him. They had quite a few Louisiana, nice actresses, and actresses. And their names
are legged sisters,
do you remember? Yeah.
Did you tell me?
Yeah, their name was legged sisters.
No, their first name.
I don't know one name, I know one's name, Melina. I don't forget all their names. It's been quite a long time ago.
But they all
were pretty Creole girls. Very pretty girls.
All were
Creole girls. So was, I don't know
Whitman sisters were Creole, but they were beautiful women too, Whitman sisters.
Oh, you told me on the old tape, I'm kind of jumping around, but I just want to clear up these things. When was the punch on the radio?

Plank was on the radio in 36. Yeah, that was when the men got the bonus. Yeah, that was in 36, huh? Well, during 30, 35, and 36 long in that time, he was playing with Francois Moses at the Rumbugie, I think it was. And then he played with Francois at this Golden Lily. Golden Lily, he played there. And they used to broadcast, and that's when he had made several records, and he would sing his records.
What was the Golden Lily like? What kind of place was it?

Well, it was a Chinese restaurant, and it was a huge place. And they had, because the Mill Brothers wasn't so famous as they are now, but they had some of the top stars. This fellow, Garbage, he used to be with Billy King. He was a comedian. And it was owned by, you know, Chinese people, and they had this lady's mistress of ceremony. Her name was Gladys Mikey.
We're about to run out already. I'm sorry, we're going to have to cut it short. It looks like this tape's just about over, and I got another appointment this afternoon.
Well, that's perfectly all right, but I would gladly be able to.
Yeah, well, we'll be back, you know, again.
I had said I was going over the river. My cousin was telling me about some fellow over the river. He's retired now, but he was... He's retired now, but he's retired now.

segments.title: Opening and the Spanish-American War song Over the Garden Wall
segments.summary: Allen opens the session at 1926 Harmony Street, 3 Sept 1960, and asks about the song Over the Garden Wall; Diggs sings it as a Spanish-American War song.

segments.title: Lions Band, Excelsior and second-line dancing in Mobile parades
segments.summary: Diggs recalls the New Orleans Lions Band coming to Mobile with more jazz than the local Excelsior, and people prancing and dancing behind the parades from about 1894-95.

segments.chapter: Growing up between Mobile and New Orleans
segments.title: First coming to New Orleans: schools and moving back and forth from Mobile
segments.summary: Diggs remembers arriving in New Orleans at five, school with white teachers, a second stay at 12-13, and returning for good after the storm; Boote adds she was born in Mobile.

segments.title: String bands versus brass bands, and when jazz reached Mobile
segments.summary: Diggs says New Orleans bands came to Mobile on excursions; Boote explains string bands played hotter music than brass bands, and that she herself grew up in New Orleans.

segments.title: Spanish-American War veterans' May celebration at Chalmette
segments.summary: Diggs describes the yearly late-May celebration the veterans attended at Chalmette.

segments.title: Benevolent societies and brass bands in Mobile parades
segments.summary: Diggs says Mobile had the same societies and Spanish-American War ceremonies, with brass bands playing a sad march at opening and closing.

segments.title: Funeral bands and jazz on the return, 'Do you rock about it'
segments.summary: Diggs says Mobile buried with bands, with fast jazz on the way back, and explains the dance called the rock about it.

segments.title: Carrie Boote's minstrel show singing: Alexander, Dying Rag, Dollar Bill
segments.summary: Boote as a girl sang in minstrel shows; she recalls fragments of Alexander, Dying Rag and Dollar Bill.

segments.title: Buddy Christian, Richard M. Jones and the uncopyrighted 'I Ain't Gonna Tell Nobody'
segments.summary: Allen and Boote talk about Buddy Christian's death, Richard M. Jones writing I Ain't Gonna Tell Nobody without copyrighting it, and Freddie Keppard.

segments.title: Glover Compton and the tune Clock of Time
segments.summary: Boote remembers pianist Glover Compton in Europe and Chicago; Allen asks about Clock of Time by Tony Jackson and Compton.

segments.title: Pianist Walter Johnson who died in India, versus Teddy Weatherford
segments.summary: Boote recalls pianist Walter Johnson, who played with Tate in Chicago and married an Indian princess; Allen suggests Teddy Weatherford.

segments.title: The Pruset brothers' Pickwick brass band of Moss Point, Mississippi
segments.summary: Boote describes Joe and Eddie Pruset's band from Moss Point, advertising dances from wagons and playing dances along the coast.

segments.title: The Whitman Sisters and spiritualism
segments.summary: Boote describes the Whitman Sisters' touring show and one sister who became a spiritualist in Chicago; Allen asks what that involves.

segments.title: Chicago New Orleans musicians: Dodds, Bill Johnson, St. Cyr, Doc Cook, Dutrey, Zutty
segments.summary: Allen runs through Chicago musicians; Boote knew of most but only knew Doc Cook and the drummer Zutty.

segments.title: The Creole 'legged sisters' and actor Ernest Whitman
segments.summary: Boote describes pretty Creole sisters from New Orleans, one married to actor Ernest Whitman, and says the Whitman sisters were Creole too.

segments.title: Punch Miller's radio broadcasts and the Golden Lily restaurant
segments.summary: Boote says Punch was on the radio in 1936 from the Rumbugie and Golden Lily, a large Chinese-owned restaurant with a mistress of ceremonies.

segments.title: Tape running out and closing
segments.summary: Allen ends the session as the tape runs out and promises to return.
